title: Thursday, Without Uniforms
excerpt: Workplace Romance · Forbidden Attraction · Slow Burn · Mature Romance
content:
Naomi changed outfits four times.

The first was too formal.

The second made her feel as though she were attending a business meeting.

The third was comfortable, which somehow seemed worse.

By the fourth outfit, she had begun to resent Devraj for making her care about a dinner that was supposed to be simple.

At six thirty, her phone buzzed.

Devraj: Still good for tonight?

She stared at the message.

Naomi: Yes.

Devraj: Excellent. I have a reservation.

Naomi: If you've booked somewhere with a twelve-course tasting menu, I'm leaving.

Devraj: I would never do that to you on your day off.

A second message arrived.

Devraj: It's only six courses.

She rolled her eyes, smiling.

The restaurant he had chosen was a small place tucked away on a quiet side street. It had warm lighting, mismatched chairs, and a menu written on a blackboard behind the counter.

It was nothing like the polished dining room where they worked.

That was precisely why she liked it.

Devraj stood when she arrived.

He was wearing a dark shirt with the sleeves rolled to his forearms, and for one disorienting second, Naomi forgot what she had planned to say.

"You look beautiful," he said.

She looked down, suddenly shy.

"Thank you."

He didn't tease her for blushing.

They ordered dinner, and for the first time since they had met, their conversation had nothing to do with tickets, customers, or service schedules.

Devraj told her about growing up in a family where every celebration revolved around food. Naomi told him about her grandmother's kitchen and the recipes she still couldn't recreate exactly.

They talked about travel, music, and the places they wanted to see.

They argued about whether a perfect meal required a perfect setting.

"It doesn't," Naomi insisted. "Give me a bowl of noodles and good company."

"Good company is doing a lot of work in that sentence."

"Don't become unbearable just because I agreed to dinner."

He laughed.

Later, when the plates had been cleared, Devraj became quieter.

"Can I tell you something?"

Naomi rested her glass on the table.

"Of course."

"When I started at the restaurant, I told myself I wasn't going to get involved with anyone there."

She raised an eyebrow.

"Really?"

"Really. Work is complicated enough without adding feelings to it."

"And yet here we are."

"Here we are."

He turned his glass slowly between his hands.

"I noticed you long before I knew anything about your rule. You were the only person in the kitchen who could be furious about a ruined sauce and still remember to ask whether the dishwasher had eaten."

Naomi looked away.

"I don't always remember."

"You do more often than you think."

He paused.

"I like how much you care. Even when it makes you difficult."

"That was almost a compliment."

"It was entirely a compliment."

She smiled, then grew serious.

"What happens if this goes wrong?"

Devraj didn't pretend not to understand.

"Then we'll have to be adults about it."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the only honest one I have. I can't promise nothing will ever hurt. I can promise I won't punish you for being honest with me."

She studied him for a long moment.

"What if I get scared and pull away?"

"Then I'll give you space. But I'd rather you tell me you're scared than disappear without a word."

The words settled between them.

Naomi had expected charm, perhaps even persuasion. She hadn't expected someone to speak so plainly about the possibility of things going wrong.

She reached across the table and touched his hand.

"I want to see where this goes," she said.

Devraj turned his palm upward, allowing her to decide whether to take it.

She did.

Outside, they walked slowly beneath the streetlights. Their hands remained linked, and the city seemed less cold than it had on the night he walked her to the station.

At the entrance to her building, Naomi stopped.

"Would you like to come up for coffee?"

His gaze searched her face.

"Coffee?"

She smiled.

"You're very literal when it suits you."

"I'm trying to behave."

"How's that working out?"

"Poorly."

She laughed, and the sound seemed to dissolve the last of the distance between them.

He leaned down and kissed her.

This time, she didn't hesitate.

She wrapped her arms around him, feeling his smile against her cheek before he kissed her again. It was warm, unhurried, and full of all the things they had spent weeks pretending not to say.

When they finally drew apart, Devraj rested his forehead against hers.

"Coffee?" he asked.

Naomi considered him.

"Coffee," she agreed.

Inside, they made it as far as the kitchen before getting distracted by another kiss.

They stayed there for a long time, talking between kisses, laughing whenever one of them tried to be serious and failed.

Eventually, Naomi leaned against the counter and studied him.

"You know the rule still exists."

"I know."

"And I haven't decided what to do about it."

"You don't have to decide tonight."

She reached for his hand.

"Good. Because I'd like you to stay a little longer."

He squeezed her fingers.

"Then I'll stay."

For once, Naomi didn't feel as though she were breaking a rule.

She felt as though she were making a choice.

And when Devraj kissed her again, she was grateful she had finally allowed herself to make it.
